This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) takes the econometric treatment of the country-year panel of the EU-frames case, the 270 rows on which the reproduction, the specification menu and the curve of the claim are built. The case takes its claim from a study by the original author (OA), who reported that poor national economic performance lowers the positive framing of the European Union [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic], and the [case study](../cases/eu-frames/index.qmd) tells it in full. The module runs from the plainest linear model through clustered standard errors and the two designs of fixed effects to random effects and the within–between model, which is where it meets the module on [multilevel models](multilevel.qmd), the treatment of the same data at the level of the respondents. It follows on from [Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html), on the AR4DS site, and assumes only what that module covers – reading a CSV, a chain of verbs joined by the pipe, and the idea of a model formula.

Every model on the page is fitted when the page is built, on the committed panel and on the small files of results that the course pipeline writes from it, so that what you read is what the code produces, and every number can be reproduced from the shipped files. The pipeline of the case, in the folder `R/eu-frames/` of the repository for the site, writes the files of results, and the [codebook of the curve](../cases/eu-frames/data/spec_curve_codebook.md) and the [codebook of the displays](../cases/eu-frames/data/displays_codebook.md) describe the columns of those files.

## 1. The country-year level {#sec-aggregation}

OA modelled individual survey respondents directly. Sixteen Eurobarometer waves pool to 416,698 people interviewed across 27 EU member states between 2004 and 2013, each asked what the European Union means to them. The core exercise of the course works instead with `EUframes_cy.csv`, which collapses the respondents to **270 country-year rows** – 27 countries observed in each of 10 years – with every framing scale averaged within the cell. For country $c$ in year $t$, the cell value is the mean of the scores of its respondents,

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \frac{1}{n_{ct}} \sum_{i \,\in\, (c,t)} y_{ict} $$

where $y_{ict}$ is the framing scale of respondent $i$ and $n_{ct}$ the number of respondents in that country-year. Unemployment and GDP growth, which are national figures to begin with, attach directly to each cell. Summing the column `n_cy` of the panel recovers the 416,698 respondents whose answers were averaged into the 270 rows, and holding the two numbers side by side, the people who were interviewed and the rows that the models analyse, makes concrete what the aggregation does.

The data are therefore nested at three levels – respondents, country-years and countries – and the [module on multilevel models](multilevel.qmd) works with all three, while this module stays at the middle level. Working there gains two things. The first is practical, and it is the reason that the course can exist at all: the raw microdata are licensed by GESIS and cannot be redistributed, whereas the derived country-year averages can be released under an open licence and shipped with the materials. The second is that the country-year is the level at which the predictor varies. Every respondent interviewed in Germany in 2010 shares one German unemployment rate for 2010, so all the information in the data about how unemployment and EU framing move together comes from 270 pairings at the country-year level, however many individuals were interviewed, and aggregating to that level discards almost none of the variation that identifies the relationship of interest.

Averaging within a cell removes all the variation between individuals inside it, so nothing about how framing differs across people of different ages, educations or outlooks survives in the panel. The standard errors no longer reflect 416,698 respondents but 270 cells, which is why the models below report residual degrees of freedom in the low hundreds rather than in the hundreds of thousands. And a relationship among country-year averages need not hold among individuals: reading an aggregate association as if it described people is the problem of ecological inference that @Robinson1950EcologicalCorrelationsBehavior set out, and the panel cannot answer the question at the level of the individual at all. Whether that matters depends on what the analysis sets out to measure, the question with which the multilevel module opens in its section on [the level of analysis](multilevel.qmd#sec-why).

The 270 rows form a balanced panel of countries, although no respondent is interviewed twice. Each Eurobarometer wave draws a new sample, so the respondents are repeated cross-sections, yet, as @Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling [p. 122] notes, "insofar as societies are units of analysis ... in an important sense the data derived from such surveys are in fact panel data, since societies are each observed multiple times". The multilevel module sets [the vocabularies of the disciplines](multilevel.qmd#sec-vocabularies) side by side, for a reader trained in one tradition who meets the terms of another.

## 2. The linear model {#sec-ols}

Every model in this module is a variation on one idea, so it pays to meet the idea in its plainest form. A **linear model** proposes that the outcome is a straight-line function of a predictor plus noise. For row $i$ of the panel the model reads

$$ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i $$

and each symbol has a plain meaning. $y_i$ is the outcome, here the mean cosmopolitan framing score of a country-year. $x_i$ is the predictor, its unemployment rate. $\beta_0$, the **intercept**, is the expected outcome when the predictor is zero. $\beta_1$, the **slope**, is the expected change in the outcome for a one-unit rise in the predictor, and it is the number on which every research question in this case depends. $\varepsilon_i$ is the **error**: everything else that moves the outcome, assumed to average out to zero. **Ordinary least squares** (OLS) estimates the two $\beta$s by choosing the line that minimises the sum of squared errors,

$$ (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1) = \underset{\beta_0,\,\beta_1}{\arg\min} \sum_i \left( y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i \right)^2 $$

which is what `lm()` (for 'linear model') computes. The name 'least squares' is meant literally, as @fig-ols-squares draws it on the course panel.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
d_std <- euframes |>
  datawizard::data_modify(x = as.numeric(scale(unemp)), y = as.numeric(scale(mcosmo)))
m_std <- lm(y ~ x, data = d_std)
d_std <- d_std |> datawizard::data_modify(fit = fitted(m_std), res = resid(m_std))
show_pts <- d_std |>
  datawizard::data_filter(abs(res) > 0.35, abs(res) < 0.95) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("x") |>
  dplyr::slice(round(seq(1, dplyr::n(), length.out = 6)))
ggplot2::ggplot(d_std, ggplot2::aes(x, y)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "grey70", size = 1.2) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(intercept = coef(m_std)[1], slope = coef(m_std)[2],
                       colour = "#0e3b6a", linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::geom_rect(data = show_pts, inherit.aes = FALSE,
                     ggplot2::aes(xmin = x, xmax = x + abs(res),
                                  ymin = pmin(y, fit), ymax = pmax(y, fit)),
                     fill = "#a10000", alpha = 0.15, colour = "#a10000", linewidth = 0.3) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(data = show_pts, ggplot2::aes(x = x, xend = x, y = fit, yend = y),
                        colour = "#a10000", linewidth = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = show_pts, colour = "#a10000", size = 1.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::coord_fixed() +
```

Nothing in that geometry is tied to a single predictor. Give the model two predictors,

$$ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 x_{2i} + \varepsilon_i $$

and the fitted object is no longer a line but a **plane** floating over the grid of the two predictors. The errors are still the vertical gaps between each point and the fitted surface, OLS still minimises the summed squares of those gaps, and each slope acquires the reading that it keeps for the rest of this module: $\beta_1$ is the expected change in the outcome for a one-unit rise in $x_1$ *with* $x_2$ *held fixed*, and 'controlling for' means no more than this movement along the plane parallel to one axis; on the panel, GDP growth is the second predictor that the specification menu can add as an adjustment.

With a third predictor the plane becomes a hyperplane that cannot be drawn, but the algebra of the arg-min never changes, and neither does the reading of a coefficient, each slope being a comparison with everything else in the model held level. The sections that follow stay with a single slope until the adjustment for growth returns with the two designs of fixed effects.

The first argument of `lm()` is a **formula**, written `outcome ~ predictor` and read "outcome as explained by predictor". The panel was read into `euframes` at the top of the page with `readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy.csv")`, the `../` being needed because this page lives in `companion/`, and fitting the model and reading it back takes two lines:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
first_model <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = euframes)
summary(first_model)
```

This output format recurs, with variations, in every model of the module, so it is worth reading slowly once. The `Call` restates the model. The `Residuals` block summarises the estimated errors $\hat\varepsilon_i = y_i - \hat y_i$, the gaps between each observed value and the fitted line. The `Coefficients` table holds the estimates themselves, one row for each $\beta$ and four columns for each row:

- **Estimate** is $\hat\beta$ itself. The `unemp` row says that a one-point rise in the unemployment rate goes with a fall of about 0.0011 in the cosmopolitan-framing score; the `(Intercept)` row says that a hypothetical country-year with no unemployment would be expected to score about 0.52.
- **Std. Error** is the standard deviation of the estimate across imagined repeated samples, which says how precisely the data pin the coefficient down. It is the denominator of the `t` value in the next column.
- **t value** is the estimate divided by its standard error, the number of standard errors by which the estimate sits from zero. It is unit-free, which is why the course can put every submitted result on one chart: whatever the scale of the model, its `t` means the same thing.
- **Pr(>|t|)** is the p-value, the probability of a `t` at least this large in magnitude if the true coefficient were zero. Small values are conventionally read as evidence that the association is not just noise.

Below the table, the **residual standard error** (0.070 here) estimates the spread of $\varepsilon$, on **268 degrees of freedom**, the 270 observations minus the two $\beta$s estimated. Degrees of freedom measure how many independent pieces of information remain for estimating uncertainty, a count that matters repeatedly later in the module. **Multiple R-squared** is the share of the variance in the outcome that the line explains, 0.4% here and so essentially nothing, and the **F-statistic** tests all the predictors at once.

Read as a whole, this first model finds no relationship worth reporting. The slope is small, its `t` of −1.04 lies well inside the range that chance produces, and its p-value is 0.30. The value recorded for the analyst C6HJR in the Multi100 dataset, on exactly these 270 rows, is a clearly negative t = −3.80, significant at the 5% level under the conventional standard errors that the analyst used, a qualification to which [section 4](#sec-inference) returns. The data are identical in both fits, so the difference lies in the structure of the model, which the rest of the module works through.

The standard errors of OLS assume that the 270 errors $\varepsilon_i$ are **independent and identically distributed**, and the estimate itself is unbiased only if the error is uncorrelated with the predictor. Both assumptions are strained here. The 270 rows are 27 countries observed ten times each, and the ten Danish rows share everything durable about Denmark. Those shared national features are part of $\varepsilon$, they are correlated within each country, and since unemployment levels also differ durably between countries, the same features are correlated with $x$ as well. The next three sections deal with each consequence in turn, first the standard errors and then the estimate itself.

## 3. Clustered standard errors {#sec-pooled}

Applied to a panel, the simple regression of section 2 has a name of its own, **pooled OLS**, because it pools all country-years into one undifferentiated cloud. Writing the same equation in the two-index notation of the panel makes the pooling visible, with one line serving every $c$ and $t$ and nothing in the model recording that rows share a country:

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ct} + \varepsilon_{ct} $$

R offers several routes to this fit, and the course materials use three of these routes: `lm()` from base R, `feols()` from the fixest package [@BergeEtAl2026FastUserfriendlyEconometrics], and `plm()` from the plm package [@CroissantMillo2023PanelDataEconometrics], the toolkit for panel econometrics that the published Multi100 analysis used. Before any new setting is introduced, a useful habit is to **make different functions agree on the model that you already understand**. If two functions give the same numbers under settings that you can name, you know what each is doing, and when the defaults of the two functions later diverge, you will know which setting moved.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_lm  <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = euframes)
m_fx  <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = euframes, vcov = "iid")
m_plm <- plm::plm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = euframes,
                  index = c("cntry", "year"), model = "pooling")

tibble::tibble(
  fitted_with = c("lm()", "feols()", "plm()"),
  estimate  = c(coef(m_lm)["unemp"], coef(m_fx)["unemp"], coef(m_plm)["unemp"]),
  std_error = c(sqrt(vcov(m_lm)["unemp", "unemp"]),
                sqrt(vcov(m_fx)["unemp", "unemp"]),
                sqrt(vcov(m_plm)["unemp", "unemp"]))
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  fitted_with estimate std_error
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>
1 lm()        -0.00110   0.00105
2 feols()     -0.00110   0.00105
3 plm()       -0.00110   0.00105
```


:::
:::


The three rows are identical to every digit, because they come from one estimator under three names: `vcov = "iid"` asks fixest for the classical standard errors that `lm()` and `plm(model = "pooling")` report by default. This like-for-like fit is the point of comparison, and the next step changes one setting only.

The first repair for the problem of correlated errors keeps the estimate and corrects its uncertainty. **Cluster-robust standard errors** replace the classical variance formula with one that permits the errors inside each cluster – here, each country – to be correlated in any pattern,

$$ \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta) \;=\; (X'X)^{-1} \Big( \textstyle\sum_{g=1}^{G} X_g' \hat\varepsilon_g^{\vphantom{\prime}} \hat\varepsilon_g' X_g^{\vphantom{\prime}} \Big) (X'X)^{-1} $$

and the notation is less fearsome than it looks. $X$ is the matrix of predictor values and $G$ the number of clusters, the 27 countries. The formula is a sandwich, whose outer 'bread' terms are the ordinary OLS ingredients while the middle 'meat' sums the residuals within each country in a way that keeps every correlation within a country intact instead of assuming it away. Only the standard error changes, and $\hat\beta$ is untouched. In the words of @CameronMiller2015PractitionersGuideClusterrobust [p. 317], whose guide is the standard reference on the subject, in such settings "default standard errors can greatly overstate estimator precision".


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# fixest: one argument
m_cl <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = euframes, cluster = ~cntry)
fixest::coeftable(m_cl)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

The two computations agree once the settings are matched. The default small-sample adjustment in fixest corresponds to `type = "HC1"` in sandwich (and to `vcovHC(..., type = "sss")` in plm), and with `type = "HC0"` the numbers would drift apart in the trailing digits, the kind of discrepancy that the like-for-like habit is there to explain. Substantively, clustering multiplies the standard error by 2.1, and the `t` falls from −1.04 to −0.50, because the 270 rows were never 270 independent pieces of evidence.

Clustering cannot rescue the estimate, and here the pooled estimate itself is the problem. Because the model absorbs no differences between countries, its slope blends two different comparisons: how framing moves when unemployment rises over time within a single country, and how framing differs between countries with high and low unemployment in the cross-section. Of the variance of unemployment on the panel, 46.5% lies between the 27 country means, as does 65.1% of the variance of the cosmopolitan share, so the cross-section carries much of the weight of a pooled fit. In these data the two comparisons point in opposite directions, and [section 5](#sec-re) estimates both, −0.0056 within countries and +0.0041 between them. The pooled slope of −0.0011 blends the two, close to zero and attached to neither comparison.

The blend is not a peculiarity of one specification. Swapped into each of the 864 specifications on the curve of the claim, with every other choice left as it was, pooled OLS puts 52.1% of the fits below zero, against 98.1% of the specifications on the curve, and the pooled fit and its twin on the curve lie on opposite sides of zero in 49.8% of the pairs. Only 7.4% of the pooled fits lie below zero with a CR2 p-value under 0.05, the test that [section 4](#sec-inference) sets out. A pooled fit therefore behaves as a different quantity rather than as a noisier version of the slope within countries; models without fixed effects are also the first of the kinds of nonequivalent model named by @Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, and pooled OLS is one of the options of the Estimator decision that the course keeps off the curve, as the [specification menu](../cases/eu-frames/menu.qmd#level-estimand) records. Clustering remains the right way to report the uncertainty of a pooled fit, but it does nothing to the sign, because the sign is a property of the estimate and not of its standard error.

## 4. Fixed effects {#sec-fe}

The second repair goes after the estimate itself. The model recorded for C6HJR in Multi100, the one that you reproduce in Task 3, is a constrained one: cosmopolitan framing regressed on the unemployment rate, with **country and year fixed effects** and nothing else,

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta\, x_{ct} + \alpha_c + \gamma_t + \varepsilon_{ct} $$

where $\alpha_c$ is a separate intercept for each country and $\gamma_t$ a separate intercept for each year. The country effects $\alpha_c$ absorb everything time-constant about a country – its language, institutions and size, and its enduring baseline level of EU enthusiasm – so the unemployment slope is identified only from how a country changes against itself over time, never from the fact that, say, Denmark and Greece differ. The year effects $\gamma_t$ take up everything common to all countries in a given year, including the shocks across the Union and the shared trajectory of the crisis. Two-way fixed effects therefore compare a country with itself over time, net of whatever moved all of Europe together in a given year.

Mechanically there are two equivalent ways to fit this model, and comparing them shows how the estimator works. The literal way estimates every intercept, putting 26 country dummies and 9 year dummies alongside the slope, and is known as the 'least squares dummy variable' route. The efficient way never estimates the intercepts at all. The **within transformation** subtracts the mean of each country and the mean of each year from both sides,

$$ \left( \bar{y}_{ct} - \bar{y}_{c\cdot} - \bar{y}_{\cdot t} + \bar{y} \right) \;=\; \beta \left( x_{ct} - \bar{x}_{c\cdot} - \bar{x}_{\cdot t} + \bar{x} \right) + \tilde\varepsilon_{ct} $$

where a dot in place of an index means 'averaged over it'. The demeaning removes the $\alpha_c$ and $\gamma_t$ from the equation, and OLS on the transformed data recovers exactly the same $\beta$:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_lsdv   <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp + factor(cntry) + factor(year), data = euframes)
m_within <- plm::plm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = euframes, index = c("cntry", "year"),
                     effect = "twoways", model = "within")
m_twfe   <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp | cntry + year, data = euframes, vcov = "iid")

c(lsdv = coef(m_lsdv)["unemp"], plm = coef(m_within)["unemp"],
  feols = coef(m_twfe)["unemp"])
```

The slope is −0.00347: within a country, a one-point rise in unemployment goes with a fall of about 0.0035 in the mean cosmopolitan-framing score, net of common yearly shocks. Its `t` is −3.80 (p = 0.0002). The two R-squared lines report different quantities. The overall adjusted R-squared of 0.72 mostly measures how much the fixed effects themselves explain, since the identities of the countries are highly predictive of framing levels, while the **within R-squared** of 0.058 is the contribution of the slope itself, with movements in unemployment explaining about 6% of the variation within countries, and only the second of the two lines bears on the research question.

The value recorded for the analyst C6HJR in the Multi100 dataset is **t = −3.804** on 233 degrees of freedom, with N = 270, which is what this model returns and what the course reproduces in Task 3.

One further point about this specification recurs on the specification menu. Grand-mean centring the predictor shifts the intercept but leaves the slope and its `t` untouched once fixed effects are present, and standardising it rescales the slope without moving its `t`, so neither form can move a point on a curve that is ranked by the partial correlation. That is why the curve holds the raw and the logged forms of unemployment and no centred or standardised twin of either.

### What the fixed effects absorb {#sec-absorb}

A fixed effect absorbs every variable that is constant within its group, whether the variable is measured or not. A country effect absorbs anything that takes one value for each country over the decade, and a year effect absorbs anything that takes one value for each year across the 27 countries. The national unemployment rate is neither, because it varies from country to country and from year to year, so both sets of effects leave it in the model and use only the part of its variation that is specific to a country-year. The fixest package makes the absorption visible when a model is given variables that the effects already contain, here the mean unemployment of each country over the decade and the mean unemployment of the 27 countries in each year:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
absorbed <- euframes |>
  dplyr::mutate(unemp_country = mean(unemp), .by = cntry) |>
  dplyr::mutate(unemp_europe = mean(unemp), .by = year)

fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp + unemp_country + unemp_europe | cntry + year,
              data = absorbed, vcov = "iid")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

The same reasoning says how much of the variation of a predictor is taken away by the year effects, namely the share of its variation within countries that is common to all countries in the same year:

```{.r .cell-code}
year_share <- c(
  unemp  = summary(lm(unemp_within ~ factor(year), data = within_country))$r.squared,
  growth = summary(lm(growth_within ~ factor(year), data = within_country))$r.squared
```

The year effects absorb 29.2% of the variation of unemployment within countries and 58.6% of the variation of growth, above all the recession of 2009, which reached every member state in the same year. A random intercept for each country, by contrast, absorbs nothing, because it is a draw from a distribution rather than a parameter for each country: it leaves a predictor that is constant within countries in the model, which is why [section 5](#sec-re) can add the country mean of unemployment to a random-effects model, and why the models of the [multilevel module](multilevel.qmd#sec-multilevel) can estimate the associations of national characteristics that fixed effects remove. Clustering absorbs nothing either, since it changes only the standard errors, as section 3 showed.

What fixed effects cannot absorb is the reason that the course builds a causal graph before choosing a specification. They do nothing about **time-varying confounding**: anything that changes within a country over the period and moves both its unemployment and its EU framing – a national political scandal, a programme of austerity specific to the country, a swing in the stance on Europe of the governing party – is absorbed by neither set of effects and can bias $\beta$. Nor do they deal with **feedback**. If EU framing itself feeds back onto economic outcomes, or if both respond to some third driver that varies over time, the model cannot detect it, and the simulations of @LeszczenskyWolbring2022HowDealReverse show how much the remedies proposed for reverse causality in panel data depend on assumptions about its timing. @Halaby2004PanelModelsSociological [p. 507] opens his review of panel models in sociology with the warning of Otis Dudley Duncan that "there is widespread, though not well articulated, opinion that in panel analysis the usual obstacles to inference and estimation are suspended for the benefit of the analyst", and the [causal-graph module](dags.qmd#sec-growth) draws the limits of fixed effects for this case.

### The two fixed-effects designs {#sec-two-designs}

The design that the analyst KQXUE fitted on the same kind of panel has an intercept for each country and none for each year. Fitted beside the two-way model, it gives a slope that is larger by more than half:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_country <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp | cntry, data = euframes, vcov = "iid")
c(two_way = coef(m_twfe)[["unemp"]], country_only = coef(m_country)[["unemp"]])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

-0.003472985 -0.005644941 
```


:::
:::


Without year effects, the comparison of a country with itself keeps the changes that every member state went through in the same year, which on this panel make up 29% of the variation in unemployment within countries. The two slopes are therefore answers to two questions rather than two estimates of one. The two-way design asks whether framing fell in a country in the years in which its unemployment rose by more than the European movement of that year, and the country design asks whether framing fell in the years in which unemployment in the country was high, whatever happened elsewhere, which leaves it open to confounding by any shift in framing across Europe that coincided with the crisis. Both are defensible readings of a claim about how national economic performance shapes framing, and the curve keeps both, as two estimands. The choice between the two designs is also the decision that divides the curve. The Estimator decision carries 41.5% of the variance of the claim-aligned partial correlation across the 864 specifications, more than any other decision, and 92.6% of the specifications with country effects alone lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against 61.8% of the two-way ones.

Two further decisions concern the predictor. The claim speaks of "poor national economic performances", and the paper measures them by unemployment and by GDP growth, so both carry the claim on the curve, each with and without the other as an adjustment. Growth has less to work with within countries, because 59% of its variation within countries is common to all of them in the same year, and the two-way design removes that common part. On the curve, 33.3% of the growth specifications lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against 82.7% of the unemployment ones. Unemployment also enters in two forms, raw, so that each percentage point counts the same, or logged, so that a rise from 4% to 8% counts as much as one from 10% to 20%, and the claim does not choose between the two forms. Among the unemployment specifications the two forms give similar shares below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, 84.4% for the raw form and 81.0% for the logged one, and the form, as a main effect, carries 0.003% of the variance. The [specification menu](../cases/eu-frames/menu.qmd#level-estimand) gives the reasoning on each option of these decisions.

### Standard errors with few clusters {#sec-inference}

The standard errors of the two-way model above, like those that the analyst reported, treat the 270 country-years as 270 independent pieces of evidence. Taking the residuals of the model country by country, and setting each beside the residual of the same country in the year before, shows that the country-years are not independent:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
resid_lag <- euframes |>
  datawizard::data_modify(e = resid(m_twfe)) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange(c("cntry", "year")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(e_before = dplyr::lag(e), .by = cntry)
rho <- cor(resid_lag$e, resid_lag$e_before, use = "complete.obs")
rho
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.530824
```


:::
:::


The residual of a country in one year correlates with its residual in the year before at 0.53, so a country that framed the EU more positively than the model expects in one year tends to do so in the next, and ten years of one country carry less information than ten independent observations would. Clustering by country, as section 3 did for the pooled model, allows any pattern of correlation within a country, and with 27 countries the clustered t is referred to G − 1 = 26 degrees of freedom. A second problem is less visible. The clustered formula works well when the clusters carry similar amounts of information, but once country and year effects are removed, the variation in unemployment that is left, which is all that identifies the slope, is concentrated in a few countries. Greece holds 17.5% of it, Spain 15.9% and Poland 10.6%, and with few clusters of such unequal weight even the clustered test overstates the evidence. @CameronMiller2015PractitionersGuideClusterrobust [p. 319] call few clusters "the most difficult complication to deal with", adding that "[t]here is no clear-cut definition of 'few'; depending on the situation, 'few' may range from less than 20 to less than 50 clusters in the balanced case".

The remedy that the course uses is the **CR2** correction of @BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard. The ordinary clustered formula takes the residuals of each country as they come out of the fit, and when one country carries much of the variation in the predictor, the fit has already been pulled towards that country, so its residuals are too small and the standard error with them. CR2 enlarges the residuals of each cluster by the amount by which the cluster has pulled the fit towards itself. Its test is then referred to a t distribution whose degrees of freedom are estimated by the Satterthwaite approximation, in the form worked out by @PustejovskyTipton2018SmallsampleMethodsClusterrobust for models with fixed effects, and those degrees of freedom say how many clusters effectively carry the information: close to G − 1 when the clusters weigh alike, far fewer when a few of them dominate. @ImbensKolesar2016RobustStandardErrors recommend this combination for few and unequal clusters, because it keeps the share of false rejections close to the 5% that the test promises, and CR2 with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom is the rule by which every point of the curve of the claim is classed. The literature on few clusters also offers a resampling answer, the wild cluster bootstrap, which flips the residuals of whole countries at random to build the distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis [@MacKinnonWebb2017WildBootstrapInference]; the course does not use it, because its only implementation in R is no longer maintained. The CR2 test takes one call to the clubSandwich package, written by Pustejovsky:

## 5. Within and between {#sec-re}

Between the pooled and the fixed-effects extremes sits a third estimator, and with it the model in which this module and the module on multilevel models meet. Its econometric name is random effects, and the multilevel tradition calls it the random-intercept model.

### Random effects {#sec-random-effects}

**Random effects** keeps a country term in the model but, rather than estimating 27 separate intercepts, treats the departures of the countries as draws from a distribution,

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ct} + u_c + \varepsilon_{ct}, \qquad u_c \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2) $$

so that instead of 27 numbers the model estimates a single one, the variance of the country effects $\sigma_u^2$. Estimation is by generalised least squares, and its mechanics place the estimator on the line that runs from pooled OLS to fixed effects. Where fixed effects subtract the *entire* mean of each country, random effects subtract a *fraction* $\theta$ of it,

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} - \theta \bar{y}_{c\cdot} = \beta_0 (1 - \theta) + \beta_1 \left( x_{ct} - \theta \bar{x}_{c\cdot} \right) + \text{error}, \qquad \theta = 1 - \sqrt{ \frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{\sigma_\varepsilon^2 + T \sigma_u^2} } $$

with $T$ the number of years for each country. At $\theta = 0$ this is pooled OLS, and at $\theta = 1$ it is fixed effects, while the data place it in between according to how much of the total variance lies between countries.

The `Effects` block is the new output to learn. The **individual** variance (0.0032) is $\hat\sigma_u^2$, the component between countries, and the **idiosyncratic** variance (0.0016) is $\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2$, the noise within them. The `share` column puts 66% of the error variance between countries. The reported $\theta$ of 0.78 places this fit 78% of the way from pooled OLS towards fixed effects, and the slope duly falls near the answer of country fixed effects, −0.0053 (z = −6.5) against the −0.0056 that country fixed effects give on their own. The default random-effects model in plm has country effects only, so its natural comparator is the one-way design of fixed effects and not the two-way one.

Random effects is more efficient than fixed effects when its central assumption holds, namely that the country effects $u_c$ are **uncorrelated with the predictor**. In econometrics that assumption has become the meaning of the term itself: "In modern econometric parlance, a random effects framework is synonymous with zero correlation between the observed explanatory variables and the unobserved effect", writes @Wooldridge2010EconometricAnalysisCross [p. 286]. Here the assumption is a strong one, because the unemployment level of a country is very likely tied up with the same durable national features that shape its baseline EU framing, the correlation that fixed effects were designed to remove. The **Hausman test** [@Hausman1978SpecificationTestsEconometrics] formalises the comparison. If the assumption held, fixed and random effects would estimate the same quantity and differ only by noise, so a large gap between the two estimates is evidence against it. Comparing the two one-way (country) estimators gives


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fe_country <- plm::plm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = euframes, index = c("cntry", "year"),
                       effect = "individual", model = "within")
re_country <- plm::plm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = euframes, index = c("cntry", "year"),
                       effect = "individual", model = "random")
hausman <- plm::phtest(fe_country, re_country)
hausman
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

data:  mcosmo ~ unemp
chisq = 9.8431, df = 1, p-value = 0.001705
alternative hypothesis: one model is inconsistent
```


:::
:::


and the test rejects (p = 0.0017), so the estimators disagree by more than chance allows and the assumption of random effects is hard to defend here. The test carries an assumption of its own, though. Its traditional form treats the random-effects estimator as efficient, which requires the errors of a country to be uncorrelated from year to year, the assumption that the residual correlation of 0.53 in section 4 rules out, and Wooldridge (p. 333) notes that without that assumption, reading the traditional statistic against its chi-squared distribution "will result in a test that will be undersized or oversized ... and we cannot generally tell which is the case". The within–between model below gives the same comparison a form that the CR2 rule of the course can test.

### The within–between model {#sec-within-between}

A more informative response than picking a winner is to split the predictor into its two kinds of variation – the *average* unemployment of each country across the decade, and the *departure* of each year from that average – and to give each its own slope. @Mundlak1978PoolingTimeSeries showed the device in its first form, which adds the country mean of the predictor to the random-effects model and keeps the predictor as it is,

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta_0 + \beta\, x_{ct} + \pi\, \bar{x}_{c\cdot} + u_c + \varepsilon_{ct} $$

and the **within–between** formulation that @BellJones2015ExplainingFixedEffects recommend enters the departure and the mean instead,

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta_0 + \beta_W \left( x_{ct} - \bar{x}_{c\cdot} \right) + \beta_B\, \bar{x}_{c\cdot} + u_c + \varepsilon_{ct} $$

where $\beta_W$ is the slope within countries and $\beta_B$ the slope between them. The two equations are one model in two parameterisations, with $\beta = \beta_W$ and $\pi = \beta_B - \beta_W$, and Bell and Jones prefer the second, among other reasons because "with temporal data it is more interpretable, as the within and between effects are clearly separated" (p. 142). The fits below use `lmer()` from lme4 [@BatesEtAl2015FittingLinearMixedeffects], the standard R package for mixed models, through lmerTest [@KuznetsovaEtAl2017LmerTestPackageTests], which adds degrees of freedom to its tests. The random-intercept term `(1 | cntry)` plays the role of $u_c$, and `datawizard::demean()` returns the country mean of a variable and the departure of each row from it.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# the country mean of unemployment (unemp_between) and the departure of each
# year from it (unemp_within)
euframes_wb <- datawizard::demean(euframes, select = "unemp", by = "cntry")

m_mundlak <- lmerTest::lmer(mcosmo ~ unemp + unemp_between + (1 | cntry), data = euframes_wb)
m_wb <- lmerTest::lmer(mcosmo ~ unemp_within + unemp_between + (1 | cntry), data = euframes_wb)

summary(m_mundlak)$coefficients
```

Read the slopes against everything fitted so far. The coefficient on unemployment in the Mundlak form and the within slope of the within–between form are the same number, −0.0056, and it is *exactly* the estimate with country fixed effects of section 4 (`m_country`), because separating out the variation between countries is what fixed effects do. The between slope is +0.0041, positive and imprecise, and the coefficient on the country mean in the Mundlak form, +0.0098, is the difference between the two slopes. The puzzle of the pooled fit in section 3 now has an arithmetic answer: the pooled slope of −0.0011 was a weighted blend of −0.0056 and +0.0041, two patterns with opposite signs averaged into a figure close to zero. And the Hausman test rejects for the same reason, because $\beta_W \neq \beta_B$: as @BellEtAl2019FixedRandomEffects [p. 1057] put it, the test, "[a]lthough often (mis)used as a test of whether FE or RE models 'should' be used ..., it is really a test of whether there is a contextual effect, or whether the between and within effects are different".

The test of $\pi$ in the Mundlak form is that comparison, and it can be carried out with cluster-robust errors, as section 4 tested the slope. The coefficients of the Mundlak form are the same when the equation is fitted by pooled OLS, which lets the CR2 rule of the course test the difference with errors clustered by country:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_mundlak_ols <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp + unemp_between, data = euframes_wb)
mundlak_cr2 <- clubSandwich::coef_test(m_mundlak_ols, vcov = "CR2", cluster = euframes_wb$cntry,
                                       coefs = "unemp_between", test = "Satterthwaite")
mundlak_cr2
```

The difference between the two slopes holds at the 5% level under the rule of the curve (p = 0.040 on 9.3 Satterthwaite degrees of freedom), as it does under the model-based errors of the within–between fit (p = 0.024), so for the cosmopolitan share and unemployment the assumption of random effects fails under every test that the course applies. The same comparison is a first encounter with the estimand, the quantity that an analysis sets out to estimate. 'The effect of unemployment on EU framing' has a value within countries and a value between them, and choosing a model means choosing which of the two you are asking for. Bell and Jones argue that this formulation should usually replace the contest between fixed and random effects, and the multilevel module reads the same model from its own side, as [a two-level model with its predictor centred within countries](multilevel.qmd#sec-rewb).

The two associations can be drawn. @fig-between-within sets the 27 country means of the cosmopolitan share against the 27 country means of unemployment, with the slope fitted across them, beside the deviations of each country-year from the means of its own country, with the slope within countries drawn through the deviations.

Across the countries the association is positive, +0.0041 per point of unemployment with p = 0.31 on 25 degrees of freedom and a correlation of 0.20 between the two sets of means, so the countries with higher unemployment over the decade did not frame the EU in less cosmopolitan terms, and if anything the pattern runs the other way. Within countries it is negative, −0.0056 with a CR2 p-value of 0.0072. The model-based test of the difference rejects the equality of the two slopes for the positive composite as well (p = 0.014), while for the utilitarian scale it gives p = 0.060. For growth both slopes of the cosmopolitan share are positive, the direction that the claim expects for growth, but only the one across countries is clearly different from zero (p = 0.009, against a CR2 p of 0.65 within countries).

These results settle the place of the options of the Estimator decision that do not hold the comparison within countries. Random effects is consistent only if the stable differences between countries are unrelated to the predictor, which the test of the two slopes rejects, and pooled OLS is a blend of the same two associations, so both stay off the curve of the claim; the within–between model would repeat points that the curve already holds, since its within slope equals the slope with country effects exactly, and its use is to show the two associations side by side, as the figure does. A reader who wants to ask the cross-national question has its answer in the regression on country means, outside the curve of the claim, and the [specification menu](../cases/eu-frames/menu.qmd#level-estimand) records the reasons for each option.

## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources}

The models of this module execute on the page from the committed course panel `EUframes_cy.csv` and the files of results that the pipeline of the case writes beside it, whose CR2 test comes from the clubSandwich package in `R/eu-frames/_curve_tools.R`, and the [data codebook](../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md) gives the country-year construction and the definitions of the items.

The estimators are those of the fixest and plm packages [@BergeEtAl2026FastUserfriendlyEconometrics; @CroissantMillo2023PanelDataEconometrics] and of lme4 [@BatesEtAl2015FittingLinearMixedeffects], and @Wooldridge2010EconometricAnalysisCross gives the econometric treatment of fixed effects, random effects, the Hausman test and the Mundlak device at length. For the same material written for sociologists, @Allison2009FixedEffectsRegression is a short introduction to fixed-effects regression and @Halaby2004PanelModelsSociological a review of panel models in sociological research. The Mundlak device goes back to @Mundlak1978PoolingTimeSeries and the specification test to @Hausman1978SpecificationTestsEconometrics; @BellJones2015ExplainingFixedEffects and @BellEtAl2019FixedRandomEffects make the case for the within–between model. On clustered errors and few clusters, @CameronMiller2015PractitionersGuideClusterrobust wrote the guide for practitioners, and the CR2 correction and its degrees of freedom come from @BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard, @PustejovskyTipton2018SmallsampleMethodsClusterrobust and @ImbensKolesar2016RobustStandardErrors, with the wild cluster bootstrap in @MacKinnonWebb2017WildBootstrapInference. The data structure of comparative surveys repeated over time is discussed by @Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling, and the problem of ecological inference was set out by @Robinson1950EcologicalCorrelationsBehavior.
